title: COVID-19 Misinformation and Social Network Crowdfunding: Cross-sectional Study of Alternative Treatments and Antivaccine Mandates
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of GoFundMe COVID-19 campaigns. Campaign narratives were manually reviewed for verifiably false claims, and shares of campaigns containing COVID-19 misinformation are reported against explicit denominators (71/133, 53%; 23/53, 43%; 48/80, 60%; 0/100 traditional). CONTENT prevalence.

estimates.country: United States (keywords queried across 50 US states)
estimates.date: Campaigns open or collecting donations September 2021–November 2021; scrape November 2021; manual review February 2022
estimates.measure_type: % of GoFundMe COVID-19 campaigns seeking funds for alternative treatments or opposing mask/vaccine mandates that contained COVID-19 misinformation
estimates.denominator: 133 manually reviewed GoFundMe campaigns: 53 expressly seeking funding for unproven/alternative COVID-19 treatments plus 80 opposing mask or vaccine mandates
estimates.definition: Campaign title, description or story contained a verifiably false or misleading statement about COVID-19 for which direct cited evidence refuting the claim could be supplied
estimates.misinfo_def: “COVID-19 misinformation was defined as ‘false or misleading statements,’ where cited evidence could be provided to refute the claim.”
estimates.source_quote: Among the small number of campaigns seeking assistance for alternative treatments and to oppose mandates, the majority (71/133, 53%) contained verified false information about COVID-19.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Manual review by the study team of every campaign in the 'Alternative Treatment' and 'Mandate' keyword categories. Only claims that could be directly refuted by cited evidence counted; each false statement is paired with a refuting reference in Table 5 (CDC/MMWR, NIH, JAMA Netw Open, etc.). Vague or unverifiable claims (e.g. personal side-effect reports) and charged language ('jab of Satan') were explicitly NOT counted. Number of reviewers and inter-rater reliability not reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: All campaigns identified by key word in the categories “Mandate” and “Alternative Treatment” were manually reviewed. ... COVID-19 misinformation for the purposes of this study adapted the standard definition of “false or misleading information meant to deceive” [ 30 ] to include only those claims where direct cited evidence could be provided to refute a claim.
estimates.notes: PRIMARY row. The denominator is a heavily selected subset (0.44% of the 30,368 analysed campaigns): only campaigns already identified as seeking alternative treatments or opposing mandates. It is NOT the prevalence of misinformation among COVID-19 crowdfunding campaigns generally — the paper never reports that figure and it would require a cross-category computation barred by R8. Rows 2 and 3 below are the two components of this row (23/53 and 48/80); pool at ONE level only, not both. breadth=false rather than misleading because the coding rule required a refutable claim and explicitly excluded unverifiable or merely rhetorical content.

estimates.country: United States (keywords queried across 50 US states)
estimates.date: Campaigns open or collecting donations September 2021–November 2021; scrape November 2021; manual review February 2022
estimates.measure_type: % of GoFundMe campaigns seeking funding for unproven/alternative COVID-19 treatments that contained COVID-19 misinformation
estimates.denominator: 53 GoFundMe campaigns expressly seeking funding for unproven or alternative COVID-19 treatments (0.17% of the 30,368 campaigns in the final analysis)
estimates.definition: Campaign narrative contained a verifiably false or misleading COVID-19 statement — chiefly advocacy of alternative treatments over vaccination or traditional treatment (n=18, 34%), pandemic-is-fake/conspiracy claims (n=2, 4%), and false claims about vaccine safety or efficacy (n=3, 7%)
estimates.misinfo_def: “COVID-19 misinformation was defined as ‘false or misleading statements,’ where cited evidence could be provided to refute the claim.”
estimates.source_quote: Alternative treatments contained COVID-19 misinformation in 23 (43%) campaigns including advocacy on alternative treatments over vaccination or traditional treatments (n=18, 34%), claims that the pandemic is not real or is a conspiracy (n=2, 4%), and false claims about the safety or efficacy of the vaccine (n=3, 7%).
estimates.page_loc: Results, Alternative Versus Traditional Treatment (also Table 3 and Abstract)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Manual review of all campaigns in the 'Alternative Treatment' keyword category; misinformation restricted to claims refutable by cited evidence, each paired with a refuting reference in Table 5. No reviewer count or reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Based on key word, there were 568 campaigns assigned to alternative treatments. After excluding those classified as “General,” “Business,” “First Response,” Traditional Treatment,” and “Mandate,” there were 53 campaigns (53/30,368, 0.17%) that were expressly seeking funding for unproven or alternative treatments for COVID-19
estimates.notes: COMPONENT of the 71/133 headline row — do not pool alongside it. Same definition, different campaign population (hence definition_variant=false). The denominator is itself a strongly self-selecting group: campaigns already asking for money for ivermectin, hydroxychloroquine, herbal remedies etc.

estimates.country: United States (keywords queried across 50 US states)
estimates.date: Campaigns open or collecting donations September 2021–November 2021; scrape November 2021; manual review February 2022
estimates.measure_type: % of GoFundMe campaigns opposing mask or vaccine mandates that contained COVID-19 misinformation
estimates.denominator: 80 GoFundMe campaigns created to oppose mask or vaccine mandates ('antirestriction'), out of 96 mandate-related campaigns (0.32% of the 30,368 analysed)
estimates.definition: Campaign narrative contained a verifiably false claim about COVID-19 or COVID-19 vaccination — masks ineffective or dangerous (n=18, 22.5%), children unaffected (n=10, 12.5%), COVID-19 mild/like a cold (n=10, 12.5%), nonvaccine prevention preferable (n=6, 7.5%), unproven treatments equally effective (n=4, 5%), pandemic fake/conspiracy (n=2, 2.5%), vaccine unsafe or ineffective (n=1, 1%)
estimates.misinfo_def: “COVID-19 misinformation was defined as ‘false or misleading statements,’ where cited evidence could be provided to refute the claim.”
estimates.source_quote: Among the 80 campaigns requesting support for antirestriction positions, 48 (60%) contained verifiably false claims regarding COVID-19 and COVID-19 vaccination.
estimates.page_loc: Results, Mandates (also Table 4: 'Contains COVID-19 misinformation, n (%) … 48 (60)')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Manual review of all campaigns in the 'Mandate' keyword category, including coding of pro- vs antirestriction stance; misinformation restricted to claims refutable by cited evidence (Table 5). No reviewer count or reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: A total of 96/30,368 (0.32%) campaigns were created to fund political positions in response to mask or vaccine mandates. Of these 93 campaigns, 80 (83%) were created to oppose restrictions (against requiring masks or vaccines; the most frequent mask mandates were in schools).
estimates.notes: COMPONENT of the 71/133 headline row — do not pool alongside it. Note the text says 'Of these 93 campaigns' where the total is given as 96 elsewhere (96 = 16 prorestriction + 80 antirestriction); the 93 appears to be a typo. The 80 denominator is used consistently in Table 4 and the Abstract, so it is safe.

estimates.country: United States (keywords queried across 50 US states)
estimates.date: Campaigns open or collecting donations September 2021–November 2021; scrape November 2021; manual review February 2022
estimates.measure_type: % of a random sample of GoFundMe COVID-19 'traditional treatment' campaigns that contained COVID-19 misinformation
estimates.denominator: Random sample of 100 campaigns drawn from the 6,391 GoFundMe campaigns in the 'Traditional Treatments' category (hospital/ICU care, medical bills, remdesivir, monoclonal antibodies, home oxygen)
estimates.definition: Campaign narrative contained a verifiably false or misleading COVID-19 statement refutable by cited evidence
estimates.misinfo_def: “COVID-19 misinformation was defined as ‘false or misleading statements,’ where cited evidence could be provided to refute the claim.”
estimates.source_quote: From the manual review of the subset (n=100) of traditional treatments, none of them contained COVID-19 misinformation.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Manual review sensitivity analysis of a random sample of 100 campaigns per non-manually-reviewed category, using the same refutable-claim criterion. No reviewer count or reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Manual review was also performed for a random sample of 100 campaigns from each other category (“Business-related,” “First Response,” “Mandate,” “Traditional Treatments,” and “General”) as a similar sensitivity analysis.
estimates.notes: The nearest thing in this paper to an unselected baseline: among ordinary COVID-19 medical-cost campaigns, misinformation prevalence was zero in a random 100. A zero-cell estimate; useful as the contrast that shows the other rows are conditioned on a selected sample. Random samples of 100 were also reviewed for 'Business-related', 'First Response' and 'General' but no misinformation counts are reported for those categories.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) 0/16 (0%) of 'prorestriction' mandate campaigns contained misinformation (Table 4, 'Contains COVID-19 misinformation, n (%): 0 (0)'; text: 'the small minority of campaigns seeking to reimpose restrictions (16) contained no COVID-19 misinformation'). Not extracted as its own row: n=16 is tiny and it is the complement of the 80-campaign antirestriction row within the same 96-campaign mandate category — an adjudicator may prefer to add it. (2) The population-level figure (71 misinformation campaigns out of 30,368 analysed, ≈0.23%) is NOT reported by the paper and would be a cross-category computation barred by R8, so no row. Likewise 53/30,368 (0.17%) alternative-treatment and 96/30,368 (0.32%) mandate campaigns are shares of campaigns on a TOPIC, not shares containing false claims, so they are not misinformation prevalence. (3) Table 5's misinformation-type counts (N=71: alternative treatment equivalent to traditional/replaces vaccination 22/31%, masks ineffective or dangerous 18/25%, children cannot get COVID-19 10/14%, COVID-19 not severe 10/14%, unsafe/experimental vaccine 6/8%, severe side effects 4/6%, pandemic fake 4/6%) are within-misinformation type shares that sum to more than 100% because campaigns could carry several claims — not prevalence rows. (4) Within-alternative-treatment misinformation rates by treatment (ivermectin 11/14 = 79%, vitamin D 3/4 = 75%, herbal 7/17 = 41%, hydroxychloroquine 0/6; Table 3) are very small cells and subdivisions of row 2; not extracted per R4. (5) All financial and engagement outcomes (funds raised, goal percentages, donors, shares) are not misinformation measures. (6) Note a probable internal inconsistency the paper does not resolve: Table 1 gives Mandate n=96 while Table 3's alternative-treatment 'Successful' total is 7 (13.2%) where the text says 6 (11%); neither affects the extracted misinformation shares.

rob.design: Cross-sectional web-scrape of GoFundMe, STROBE-reported. Frame: 24 COVID-19/unproven-treatment keywords queried across 50 US states (1,200 searches) in November 2021 for campaigns open or collecting donations Sept–Nov 2021; 126,695 campaigns identified, 30,368 (24.0%) met final criteria; campaigns open <30 days excluded. Keywords derived from CDC/WHO/Wikipedia/WebMD/Mayo/Johns Hopkins myth lists and finalised with an expert author. Campaigns assigned to six a priori categories by keyword with a stated hierarchy; ALL 'Alternative Treatment' and 'Mandate' campaigns manually reviewed, plus a random 100 from each other category as sensitivity analysis. No response rate (platform data). Misinformation coding required a refutable claim with a supplied reference; number of coders and inter-rater reliability NOT reported — the main reliability weakness. Limitations acknowledged: single time frame, long and heterogeneous campaign date range (2011–2021), 'alternative treatment' definition borrowed from one prior study.
rob.item6_quote: COVID-19 misinformation for the purposes of this study adapted the standard definition of “false or misleading information meant to deceive” [ 30 ] to include only those claims where direct cited evidence could be provided to refute a claim. For each misleading statement, a reference is provided to directly refute this claim. Vague claims or those that could not be possible to prove false were not considered misinformation.
rob.item10_quote: Moreover, 23 (43%) of the 53 campaigns seeking support for alternative treatments contained COVID-19 misinformation. There were 80 campaigns that opposed mandating masks or vaccination, 48 (60%) of which contained COVID-19 misinformation.
